content: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a condition affecting the developing retina in preterm infants, characterized by abnormal growth of retinal blood vessels. This abnormal proliferation can lead to severe visual impairment or even retinal detachment, despite available treatments. Despite significant advancements in neonatal care over the past decades, ROP remains a leading cause of childhood vision loss globally. Infants with milder forms of ROP are also at increased risk for long-term visual complications, such as myopia, strabismus, and amblyopia. In high-resource countries, severe ROP is predominantly seen in extremely preterm infants. For example, in a multicenter study in the United States, 60% of infants born between 22 and 28 weeks of gestation were diagnosed with ROP, with 15% having stage 3 or more severe disease. The incidence of severe ROP decreases with increasing gestational age. Infants born at 32 weeks or later are at very low risk for ROP, and those born after 28 weeks typically develop mild disease that does not require treatment. Conversely, in low-resource settings with developing neonatal care systems, ROP is more frequently observed in larger and more mature preterm infants. The global incidence of ROP varies depending on local rates of preterm birth, survival, and standards of neonatal care. ROP, insufficient screening, and lack of treatment pose significant threats to vision in preterm infants. In 2010, approximately 170,000 preterm infants worldwide developed some degree of ROP, with 54,000 cases being severe and potentially blinding. However, only 42% of these severe cases received necessary treatment. Normal retinal vascular development is driven by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), a protein regulated by oxygen levels. After birth, exposure to the relatively high-oxygen environment outside the womb can suppress VEGF production, halting blood vessel growth. This stage, known as phase I ROP, is followed by a period of relative retinal hypoxia as the infant grows, leading to overproduction of VEGF and abnormal neovascularization, characteristic of phase II ROP. Several factors that support VEGF-mediated retinal vascular growth in utero are absent after preterm birth, contributing to phase I ROP. One critical factor is insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which is primarily derived from maternal sources during pregnancy but is synthesized in the preterm liver after birth. IGF-1 facilitates VEGF activity, promoting normal retinal vessel growth. However, in preterm infants, serum IGF-1 levels often drop significantly due to extreme prematurity, reduced omega-3 fatty acids, or other nutritional deficiencies. This decline contributes to the cessation of vessel growth in phase I ROP. As the infant grows, IGF-1 levels gradually increase, and the retina's hypoxic state can lead to excessive VEGF production, resulting in the abnormal neovascularization of phase II ROP. Given the frequency and potential severity of ROP, regular retinal screening is essential for preterm infants. However, global access to ROP screening is inconsistent. A survey of 194 countries found that only 35% had established screening programs with defined criteria. Many countries in Africa and Southeast Asia lack screening programs entirely, while others have limited or poorly understood screening practices. In countries with screening programs, criteria vary. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends regular retinal examinations for infants born at ≤30 weeks of gestation, weighing <1500 grams at birth, or weighing 1500–2000 grams with an unstable hospital course and increased risk of ROP. Predictive models incorporating postnatal weight gain, IGF-1 levels, and other factors may improve the targeting of high-risk infants for screening. The severity of phase II ROP varies in location, extent, and severity. Ophthalmologists use the International Classification of ROP to describe findings. Treatment is recommended when ROP meets criteria defined by the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) study, referred to as Type I ROP. Current treatments include physical destruction of the avascular retina and VEGF-blocking agents. Retinal ablation interrupts ROP progression by destroying VEGF-overproducing tissue. Cryotherapy was the first large-scale treatment for severe ROP, improving outcomes compared to no intervention. Laser photocoagulation later replaced cryotherapy due to its technical ease, precision, and reduced side effects. Laser treatment for Type I ROP reduces unfavorable outcomes, such as retinal detachment and blindness, compared to delayed treatment. However, laser photocoagulation is invasive, expensive, and results in permanent peripheral vision loss. Treated eyes remain at risk for adverse outcomes, with 25% experiencing unfavorable visual outcomes and 9% having unfavorable structural outcomes at six years of follow-up. Additionally, the personnel and equipment required for laser treatment may not be available in all countries. VEGF-blocking agents are being actively investigated as treatments for severe ROP, either alone or in combination with laser ablation. Bevacizumab, a monoclonal antibody that inhibits VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, is increasingly used outside research settings. Bevacizumab may be more effective than laser photocoagulation for severe ROP in the posterior retina. It also reduces the recurrence of ROP compared to laser treatment, though recurrence may occur later, necessitating prolonged follow-up. The optimal dosage, systemic side effects, and follow-up duration for bevacizumab therapy remain uncertain. Other investigational therapies, such as inositol, are also under study. The intervention under review is the postpartum administration of recombinant human IGF-1 via continuous intravenous infusion. Preterm infants with ROP have lower serum IGF-1 levels than age-matched infants without retinal disease. Restoring IGF-1 to normal levels early in retinal development may prevent ROP. A feasibility study demonstrated that recombinant human IGF-1 could be administered as a continuous infusion, with doses individualized to maintain serum IGF-1 within physiological intrauterine levels (20–60 mcg/L). Among nine treated infants, the mean dose was 95.1 mcg/kg/day, and the mean infusion duration was 14.2 days. By restoring IGF-1 to in utero levels, this therapy may interrupt phase I ROP pathogenesis, preventing the proliferative neovascularization of phase II ROP. Phase I trials of IGF-1 replacement have been conducted, and phase II trials are ongoing, comparing IGF-1 infusion to no treatment. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials will provide summarized results, contributing to the optimal management of ROP in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants.
